Exercise 2.1 · Week 2

Pet Class

Python in Thonny Work in pairs

Goal: finish the Pet class - a blueprint for virtual pets - and make two pets that each keep their own numbers.

  1. Open starter.py in Thonny. Read __init__ and feed: they are done.
  2. Finish the TODOs in play, mood and describe.
  3. Press Run. Type p a few times, then f. Watch Pip change while Bo stays the same.

Done looks like:

Pip the dragon feels okay.
f = feed Pip, p = play with Pip, q = quit: p
Pip the dragon feels happy. (hunger 6, happiness 7)
Bo the robot cat feels okay. <- Bo did not change: a different object!

Extra: add a nap() method (happiness +1), or a third pet. Keep it kind: your pet should never get sick or blame the player.

Starter code

Open starter.py in Thonny, or copy the code below into a new file and save it as starter.py.

# Pet Class - YOUR version
# A class is a blueprint. Every Pet object made from it has its OWN numbers.
# Kind design: our pets never get sick, run away or make you feel guilty.
# Finish the TODOs, then press Run and see if it does what the README says.


class Pet:
    """Blueprint for a virtual pet."""

    def __init__(self, name, species):
        # __init__ runs once, when a new pet is made. self is "this pet".
        self.name = name
        self.species = species
        self.hunger = 5      # 0 = full, 10 = very hungry
        self.happiness = 5   # 0 = bored, 10 = very happy

    def feed(self):
        """Feeding makes the pet less hungry (never below 0). (Already done!)"""
        self.hunger = self.hunger - 3
        if self.hunger < 0:
            self.hunger = 0

    def play(self):
        """Playing makes the pet happier (max 10) and a little hungrier (max 10)."""
        # TODO 1: add 2 to self.happiness, but never go above 10
        # TODO 2: add 1 to self.hunger, but never go above 10
        pass

    def mood(self):
        """Return one word that describes how the pet feels right now."""
        # TODO 3: return "hungry" if hunger is 7 or more,
        #         otherwise "happy" if happiness is 7 or more,
        #         otherwise "bored" if happiness is 3 or less,
        #         otherwise "okay"
        return "okay"

    def describe(self):
        """Return a sentence about the pet, like 'Pip the dragon feels okay.'"""
        # TODO 4: use an f-string with self.name, self.species and self.mood()
        return ""


if __name__ == "__main__":
    pip = Pet("Pip", "dragon")
    bo = Pet("Bo", "robot cat")
    print(pip.describe())
    print(bo.describe())
    while True:
        choice = input("f = feed Pip, p = play with Pip, q = quit: ").strip().lower()
        if choice == "q":
            print("Bye! Pip and Bo will be fine until next time.")
            break
        if choice == "f":
            pip.feed()
        elif choice == "p":
            pip.play()
        print(pip.describe(), f"(hunger {pip.hunger}, happiness {pip.happiness})")
        print(bo.describe(), "<- Bo did not change: a different object!")

Stuck? Open a hint

Try on your own first. Hints open one at a time, from a small nudge to a bigger one. None of them gives the answer away.

Hint 1: Where to look

Read feed first, since it is already done. It adds or subtracts, then stops the number from going too far. play works the same way. Each pet keeps its own hunger and happiness.

Hint 2: Try this

In play, change self.happiness with an if that caps it at 10, then do the same for self.hunger. In mood, use if statements in the order the comments list. A return ends the function straight away. In describe, use an f-string.

Hint 3: Almost there

For the cap, copy the shape of feed: self.happiness = self.happiness + ____, then if self.happiness > ____: and set it back to the limit. For the sentence, use return f"____" and put {self.____} pieces inside it. Call the method with self.mood().
